c: means the rules that keep a shared project safe and understandable when many people work on it. In dbt, the main idea is simple: some models are a
(the team that builds and owns it) and
(the people, dashboards, notebooks, Python models and other dbt projects that read it).

A producer wants freedom: refactor the SQL, rename internal models, change the logic. A consumer wants stability: the columns they use today must still be there tomorrow, with the same type. Governance is the agreement between the two.
Think of a restaurant. The kitchen (the producer) can reorganise its shelves, change suppliers and train new cooks every week: this is

. The menu (the public interface) is a promise to the customers: if the menu says "soup of the day, 250 ml, hot", the customers must get exactly that. When the restaurant wants to change the menu in a big way, it prints a

menu, keeps the old dishes for a few weeks, and puts a note: "this dish disappears on 30 June". Access is the kitchen door, the contract is the menu, constraints are the food-safety rules checked by the inspector (the data platform), and versions are the new menu with its end date.

A contract is like the shape of an electric socket. The plug (the query) must have exactly the right pins (columns) with the right form (types). dbt checks the plug
it pushes it in. A plug with one pin too many or one pin missing is refused, even if it would "mostly work".
With an enforced contract, dbt changes the way it builds a table. Without a contract, a table model is one statement:
. With a contract, dbt first runs a
, then builds the table in two steps.

blocks.alt: How dbt enforces a model contract, in four steps: 1. Query shape: the model SQL runs with where false limit 0 and dbt reads its names and types. 2. Contract shape: dbt builds cast(null as <data_type>) for each YAML column and reads the types. 3. Compare: names and types, order ignored; any mismatch is an error and nothing is built. 4. Build: create table with the types and constraints, then insert the rows.

. Versions are worth the effort when people or systems outside your team depend on the model; for a model only your team uses, just change it and update the consumers in the same pull request.

A version is like a new edition of a textbook. The second edition changes the chapter numbers, so the teacher announces: "From September we use edition 2. Edition 1 is still accepted until June." Students who already bought edition 1 have time to change, and nobody wakes up with the wrong page numbers.
